situation:
You are the marketing manager at TWIN MAPLE YOGURT CO., a self-serve frozen yogurt chain with thirty-one shops and the largest share of its home state. The company is opening its first shop across the state line this year. The vice president of marketing (judge) has asked you to bring a recommendation to a meeting this week.

The company signed a letter of intent on a strip-mall space near the new city's university. Since then CHILL HOUSE, a national self-serve competitor, has opened two blocks from that space, with a heavier opening budget than the company had planned to spend and the same toppings-by-weight format.

A crosstown site has come open next to a transit stop. Counts taken there over three weekends show more than twice the foot traffic of the university space. A former employee already runs a licensed TWIN MAPLE YOGURT CO. shop a mile from that site, under a license promising no company shop within three miles of hers.

Taking the crosstown site would put the company in front of the traffic it needs to build a clientele from opening week, but it breaks the three-mile promise to the licensed operator, and the site's back room holds one small freezer, too little to store the yogurt mix properly between deliveries three times a week.

Keeping the university space and outspending CHILL HOUSE on the opening costs the promotion budget set aside to build that shop's first year of regulars, and the two shops would still be splitting the same students. The vice president of marketing (judge) wants your reading of the new market and a recommendation on the site. The vice president of marketing (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the vice president of marketing (judge) at TWIN MAPLE YOGURT CO. Business background is the same as the situation above. You approved the letter of intent on the university space, you signed the license the former employee operates under, and you have seen the weekend traffic counts from the crosstown site. You want the marketing manager to give you a reading of the new market and to recommend which site the first out-of-state shop should take.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and listen to the presentation without steering it. After the presentation, ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What is the first thing we would do if we go with your recommendation?
Who has to be told, and in what order?
